cards.title: John Wilby
cards.body: London met the 14-minute ambulance standard on 64 per cent of calls; the expectation was 95. CAD was bought to close that gap. Two days after go-live Virginia Bottomley told the Commons that South West Thames RHA had accepted John Wilby's resignation as LAS chief executive; Martin Gorham took over.
cards.prompt: Two days after the despatch system went live, who lost his job over it — and what was the performance gap the Commons was told about the same afternoon?
cards.answer: John Wilby, chief executive of the London Ambulance Service; South West Thames RHA accepted his resignation on 28 October 1992. Virginia Bottomley told the Commons London was responding within 14 minutes on 64 per cent of calls against an expected 95 per cent.

cards.title: The exception queue, 26-27 October 1992
cards.body: Demand was below October's average and the computer did not fail in a technical sense; the exception-message queue simply grew past what the operators could clear. The winning consortium bid had been £937,463, some £700,000 cheaper than the next nearest. By the next afternoon London was dispatching ambulances off printouts.
cards.prompt: Nothing crashed and the day was quieter than average. Name the quantity that was actually failing, and the price paid for the system that hid it.
cards.answer: Queue length — the exception-message backlog, not CPU or uptime. The winning Apricot/Systems Options/Datatrak bid was £937,463, about £700,000 under the next nearest bid.

cards.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service
cards.sub: February 1993 · South West Thames Regional Health Authority
cards.body: ISBN 0 905133 70 6. Section 4 draws the reinforcing loop as a cause-and-effect diagram: bad status data, bad allocations, more exception messages, a slower system, more call backs, more delay. Its verdict on the machine itself is that it "did what it had been designed to do".
cards.prompt: Where do you read the primary account of this failure, and which part of it draws a reinforcing loop instead of naming a bug?
cards.answer: The February 1993 Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service, South West Thames RHA, ISBN 0 905133 70 6 — Section 4, "Causes and Effects of Breakdown on 26 and 27 October 1992", paragraphs 4016-4032.

cards.title: The second buffer
cards.body: From the afternoon of 27 October the control room ran semi-manual. Shortly after 2am on 4 November the system slowed, then locked up. A Systems Options programmer had left code that took a little file-server memory on every vehicle mobilisation and never released it; three weeks of mobilisations used all of it. LAS went to paper.
cards.prompt: The service limped along semi-manually for a week, then the system died for good in the early hours of 4 November 1992. What killed it, and why is that the same failure shape twice?
cards.answer: A memory leak: code left in three weeks earlier took file-server memory on every vehicle mobilisation and never freed it, until memory ran out and the system locked up. Both failures were an unwatched quantity growing without bound — first the despatch queue, then the heap.
